claim: Amazon CloudWatch monitors your AWS resources and the applications you run on AWS in real time, and offers tools for system-wide observability of application performance, operational health and resource utilization.
v: monitors your Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch

Amazon CloudWatch monitors your Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources and the applications you run on AWS in real time, and offers many tools to give you system-wide observability of your application performance, operational health, and resource utilization.

claim: CloudWatch provides two types of metrics: OpenTelemetry Metrics, which the documentation marks as recommended, and CloudWatch Metrics (Classic).
q: What two types of metrics does CloudWatch provide?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch
CloudWatch provides two types of metrics: OpenTelemetry Metrics (recommended) and CloudWatch Metrics (Classic).

claim: Many AWS services automatically report metrics into CloudWatch, and you can also publish your own custom metrics with OpenTelemetry (OTLP) or with the PutMetricData API.
q: How do metrics get into CloudWatch?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch
Many AWS services automatically report metrics into CloudWatch, and you can also publish your own custom metrics, either with OpenTelemetry (OTLP) or with the PutMetricData API.

claim: CloudWatch provides curated automatic dashboards for many AWS services so that you do not have to build them yourself.
q: Do you have to build a dashboard for each AWS service by hand?
v: don't have to build them yourself
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch
CloudWatch provides curated automatic dashboards for many AWS services, so that you don't have to build them yourself.

claim: Many AWS services offer basic monitoring by publishing a default set of metrics to CloudWatch at no charge, and basic monitoring is enabled automatically when you start using such a service.
q: Is basic monitoring on by default and is it free?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-metrics-basic-detailed

Many AWS services offer basic monitoring by publishing a default set of metrics to CloudWatch with no charge to customers. By default, when you start using one of these AWS services, basic monitoring is automatically enabled.

claim: Detailed monitoring is offered by only some services, it incurs charges, and you must choose to activate it for an AWS service.
q: Is detailed monitoring on by default and is it free?
v: you must choose to activate it
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-metrics-basic-detailed
Detailed monitoring is offered by only some services. It also incurs charges. To use it for an AWS service, you must choose to activate it.

claim: Amazon EC2 detailed monitoring publishes metrics at one-minute intervals, instead of the five-minute intervals used in EC2 basic monitoring.
q: How often does EC2 publish metrics with basic and with detailed monitoring?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-metrics-basic-detailed
For example, Amazon EC2 detailed monitoring provides more frequent metrics, published at one-minute intervals, instead of the five-minute intervals used in Amazon EC2 basic monitoring.

claim: Detailed monitoring has different names in different services: detailed monitoring in Amazon EC2, enhanced monitoring in AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and request metrics in Amazon S3.
q: What is detailed monitoring called in Elastic Beanstalk and in Amazon S3?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-metrics-basic-detailed

In different AWS services, detailed monitoring also has different names. For example, in Amazon EC2 it is called detailed monitoring, in AWS Elastic Beanstalk it is called enhanced monitoring, and in Amazon S3 it is called request metrics.

claim: Application Signals automatically detects and monitors an application's key performance indicators such as latency, error rates and request rates, without manual instrumentation or code changes.
q: Which CloudWatch feature gives application performance monitoring without code changes?
v: without manual instrumentation or code changes
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch

With Application Signals you can automatically detect and monitor your applications' key performance indicators like latency, error rates, and request rates without manual instrumentation or code changes.

claim: CloudWatch Synthetics runs configurable scripts called canaries that simulate user behavior to monitor your endpoints and APIs and alert you to availability issues or performance degradation before they affect real users.
q: Which CloudWatch feature checks endpoints on a schedule like a customer would?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch

CloudWatch Synthetics complements this by enabling you to proactively monitor your endpoints and APIs through configurable scripts called *canaries* that simulate user behavior and alert you to availability issues or performance degradation before they impact real users.

claim: Canaries are configurable scripts that run on a schedule and follow the same routes and perform the same actions as a customer, so you can verify the customer experience even when you have no customer traffic.
q: Can a canary verify availability when there is no real traffic?
v: configurable scripts that run on a schedule
even when you don't have any customer traffic
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch_Synthetics_Canaries

You can use Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics to create *canaries*, configurable scripts that run on a schedule, to monitor your endpoints and APIs. Canaries follow the same routes and perform the same actions as a customer, which makes it possible for you to continually verify your customer experience even when you don't have any customer traffic on your applications.

claim: CloudWatch RUM performs real user monitoring: it collects and shows client-side performance data of web and mobile applications from actual user sessions in near real time.
q: Which CloudWatch feature measures performance from real user sessions in the browser or app?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-RUM
With CloudWatch RUM, you can perform real user monitoring to collect and view client-side data about your web and mobile application performance from actual user sessions in near real time.

claim: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) in CloudWatch let you define, track and alert on specific reliability targets for your applications, using error budgets and SLO compliance over time.
q: How do you track a reliability target such as availability in CloudWatch?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch

Use Service Level Objectives (SLOs) in CloudWatch to define, track, and alert on specific reliability targets for your applications, helping you maintain service quality commitments by setting error budgets and monitoring SLO compliance over time.

claim: Database Insights lets you monitor database performance metrics in real time, analyze SQL query performance and troubleshoot database load for AWS database services.
q: Which CloudWatch feature analyzes SQL query performance for AWS databases?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch
Database Insights allows you to monitor database performance metrics in real time, analyze SQL query performance, and troubleshoot database load issues for AWS database services.

claim: Lambda Insights provides system-level metrics for Lambda functions, including memory and CPU utilization tracking and cold start detection and analysis.
q: Which CloudWatch feature shows memory and CPU use and cold starts for Lambda functions?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch
Lambda Insights provides system-level metrics for Lambda functions, including memory and CPU utilization tracking, and cold start detection and analysis.
